::: {.lead}
We're introducing **River 1.0**, the first Marketing Foundation Model from PyMC Labs and
the first network for the PyMC MFM library. River reads one weekly marketing table
(spend per channel, controls and sales) and returns draws of every contribution, with
the causal graph behind each draw. It needs no new parameter fit: it learned from
200,000 simulated marketing worlds with known answers, and its weights stay fixed for
every new dataset.
:::

::: {.mfm-note}
**Research preview**

All of River's tests use simulated data with known truth, and validation against real-world incrementality tests remains open.
:::

| At a glance | |
|:--|:--|
| Parameters | 2.4M |
| Simulated training worlds | 200,000 |
| Median first answer for one query week | 1.25 s |
| Comparisons with a majority of paired wins | 11 of 15 |

## What River does {#what}

Give River a weekly table: spend for each channel, control variables such as price or
promotions, and sales. For every week it returns the part of sales that came from the
baseline, from each channel and from each control, as draws, so each part has an
uncertainty interval. The table can continue past the last observed sales: supply spend
and controls for those weeks and River decomposes them too. Weeks with sales are
*context*; weeks without are the *query*.

Each draw also carries a causal graph: which inputs have a direct effect on sales. A
conventional marketing mix model fixes one structure; River averages over the
structures its training allowed, including inputs that are present but have no effect.
You can also take the most frequent graph, or fix your own.

River rescales every series with statistics of its context weeks, so sales, spend and
controls can be in any units. After conversion back, the estimates differ only by
numerical rounding.

## How River was trained {#training}

**The prior.** A simulator writes down the assumptions: how spend carries over, how
response saturates, how the baseline moves, and which inputs drive sales. From it we
drew 200,000 accepted worlds of 208 weeks: 196,000 for training and 4,000 held out. The
prior mixes 50 equally weighted combinations: five response shapes, including a linear
one, each with or without geometric carryover, times five input settings (calm,
hectic, mixed, spiky inputs and a hectic baseline). A world has 1 to 10 channels and
1 to 10 controls, and an input that is present need not affect sales. No real company
data were used.

**The network.** A transformer encoder reads the weekly table. A router samples a
complete graph of direct effects, a graph conditioner adapts the encoder's
representations to that graph, and a conditional decoder turns fresh noise into
contribution draws. Conditional flow matching trains the network to carry noise to
samples; at inference, sixteen fixed Euler steps do the carrying.

| Spec | |
|:--|:--|
| Parameters | 2,443,583 |
| Encoder | 4 blocks, width 128, 8 attention heads, feed-forward 512 |
| Flow networks | two hidden layers of 256 (SiLU) |
| Training worlds | 200,000 × 208 weeks (196,000 train, 4,000 held out) |
| Context lengths | 75 to 207 weeks |
| Optimisation | 62,500 AdamW updates of 64 views (3.4 epochs) |
| Hardware | one NVIDIA H100 |
| Bundle | about 10 MB, 10 control slots |

## Benchmarks {#benchmarks}

We tested River on 500 cases with known truth: five conditions of 100 held-out worlds.
Three conditions follow the training assumptions (all inputs, a logistic saturation
response, a smoothly varying baseline). Two hide information: the channel or the
control with the largest effect. Each case is read at three splits, with 99, 185 or
207 weeks of sales to estimate the next 109, 23 or one week: 1,500 scored views.

The references are PathMC with carryover and saturation, ordinary least squares (OLS),
and a PyMC-Marketing MMM with default settings. The score is the continuous ranked
probability score (CRPS) of each input's contribution over the query weeks; it judges
the whole distribution, and lower is better.

Across all five conditions and all three horizons, River's mean channel and control
scores are lower than those of PathMC and OLS. On the same world, River beats both in a
majority of worlds in 11 of the 15 condition-and-horizon comparisons for channels.

A separate test compares River with the configured PyMC-Marketing MMM on 100 full-input
worlds at the three horizons. The MMM's mean error is a multiple of River's:

| Contribution | MMM error vs River |
|:--|:--|
| Channel contributions | 2.1–2.4× |
| Control contributions | 5.4–5.7× |
| Baseline | 4.0–5.1× |

These are ratios of cohort means, not typical world-level ratios, and the MMM fits
include runs that failed sampler diagnostics. They do not establish an advantage over
converged Bayesian MMMs in general.

## Speed {#speed}

River needs no new fit, so a new dataset gets an answer as soon as the network has
read it. In the timing test (100 twelve-channel worlds), River ran on a GPU and the
MMM on eight CPU cores:

```{=html}
<figure class="mfm-chart">
<figcaption><strong>Time to the first answer</strong><span>Median seconds, log scale. MMM time is a fresh fit plus its first prediction.</span></figcaption>
<svg viewBox="0 0 400 170" role="img" aria-label="Median time to the first answer, log scale. One query week: River 1.25 seconds, MMM fit plus first prediction 387.30 seconds. 109 query weeks: River 113.78 seconds, MMM 238.66 seconds."><text class="gl" x="0" y="12">One query week</text><text class="lb" x="0" y="43">River 1.0</text><rect x="82" y="32" width="7.6" height="14" rx="2" fill="#b4e7dd"/><text class="vl" x="97.6" y="43">1.25 s</text><text class="lb" x="0" y="67">MMM</text><rect x="82" y="56" width="203.7" height="14" rx="2" fill="#8593ab"/><text class="vl" x="293.7" y="67">387.30 s</text><text class="gl" x="0" y="104">109 query weeks</text><text class="lb" x="0" y="135">River 1.0</text><rect x="82" y="124" width="161.9" height="14" rx="2" fill="#b4e7dd"/><text class="vl" x="251.9" y="135">113.78 s</text><text class="lb" x="0" y="159">MMM</text><rect x="82" y="148" width="187.1" height="14" rx="2" fill="#8593ab"/><text class="vl" x="277.1" y="159">238.66 s</text></svg>
<p class="mfm-chart__note">Latency grows with query length. Once fitted, the MMM answers a warm 109-week query in about 4 s, faster than River's 114 s. Times exclude River's one-off training.</p>
</figure>
```

Smaller problems are quicker. With the library's quickstart world (two channels,
42 query weeks), 1,000 draws took 2.0 s on an Apple M3 Max CPU.

## Causal structure {#structure}

River samples which inputs have a direct effect. Within its training prior, on 100
full-input worlds:

| Measure | Result |
|:--|:--|
| Precision and recall for active channels | ≈ 90% |
| Worlds with the complete active-channel set recovered | 45–51% |
| Worlds with the true graph among 2,048 drawn graphs | 82–86 of 100 |

This is partial recovery inside the permitted family of direct effects, not
unrestricted causal discovery. Selecting the one correct graph remains harder than
covering it.

## Limits {#limits}

- **Simulation only.** River is tested on simulated worlds with known truth. A
  separate study approximates two observed marketing collections, which does not
  establish accuracy on observed business data. Do not use River alone for budget
  decisions.
- **Calibration is open.** River gives intervals for every contribution, but
  long-query contribution intervals under-cover. Calibration and validation come
  before intervals can support budget decisions.
- **Contributions, not forecasts.** Lower contribution error does not mean better
  total-sales prediction: for one-week totals, the fitted references score better.
- **Direct effects only.** The current weights support direct effects on sales, and
  1 to 10 channels as trained.

## Get River {#get}

River ships as the profile `river-1` of the Hugging Face repository `pymc-labs/mfm`,
currently private to the PyMC Labs organisation. Log in with `hf auth login` (or set
`HF_TOKEN`), then load it at its pinned commit:

```bash
pip install "pymc-mfm[hub] @ git+https://github.com/pymc-labs/pymc-mfm.git"
```

```python
from pymc_mfm import from_pretrained

model = from_pretrained(
    "pymc-labs/mfm",
    profile="river-1",
    revision="970e6095f14824d7e25ecace7e20a47bebde35b8",
)
```
